subsystems.name: Pusher plate and shock absorbers
subsystems.role: the actual engine: it converts the blast of each detonation into a smooth push.
parts: thick steel or aluminium plate tens of metres across
thrust ring tied into the vehicle spine

subsystems.name: Pulse units
subsystems.role: metered nuclear charges shaped to throw most of their energy rearward at the plate rather than sideways.
parts: channel filler that turns to directed plasma

subsystems.name: Magazine and ejection system
subsystems.role: stores the charges and fires them out to a fixed standoff distance at a steady rate.

subsystems.name: Thrust vectoring and attitude control
subsystems.role: keeps the plate square to the thrust axis and steers by offsetting pulses or using small thrusters.

subsystems.name: Shadow shield and crew/payload protection
subsystems.role: stops neutrons and gamma rays from reaching people and electronics.
parts: shadow shield between magazine and crew

subsystems.name: Thermal and structural spine
subsystems.role: ties plate, magazine and payload together and dumps the heat each pulse deposits.

buildSteps.title: Fix the mission budget
buildSteps.detail: Choose a target velocity change, then work out how many pulses and how much mass that implies. Unlike a chemical rocket, thrust is set by pulse rate and plate size, not by a combustion chamber.

buildSteps.title: Design the pulse unit
buildSteps.detail: Size a small device of roughly 0.1–1 kilotonne yield and surround it with a heavy filler so the energy leaves as a narrow plasma jet aimed at the plate.

buildSteps.title: Build the pusher plate
buildSteps.detail: Fabricate a very thick steel or aluminium disc and mount it on long-stroke shock absorbers. These must stretch a millisecond impulse of thousands of tonnes of force into an acceleration the structure and crew can survive.

buildSteps.title: Assemble magazine and ejection gun
buildSteps.detail: Build an armoured magazine that feeds units to a gun firing them rearward about once per second, with interlocks that prevent a detonation too close to the plate.

buildSteps.title: Add shielding and control
buildSteps.detail: Fit a shadow shield on the vehicle axis so the plate itself blocks line-of-sight radiation, and install the timing computer that keeps pulses centred.

buildSteps.title: Validate with conventional explosives
buildSteps.detail: Test the plate and shock absorbers using chemical charges, as the Project Orion studies did in 1959. This proves the mechanical coupling without any nuclear yield.

buildSteps.title: Test a low-yield pulse in space
buildSteps.detail: Flight validation requires detonating a device in vacuum — which the 1963 Partial Test Ban Treaty and 1967 Outer Space Treaty prohibit, so no such test has ever been flown.

buildSteps.title: Assemble in orbit and fly
buildSteps.detail: Because a pulse vehicle is enormous, sections would be launched separately and joined in orbit before the first pulse is fired.

buildSteps.title: Scale to a deep-space or interstellar precursor
buildSteps.detail: With the plate and pulse unit proven, thrust scales with pulse rate and yield, giving velocities of thousands of kilometres per second.

prerequisites.tech: Compact nuclear devices with shaped, directed output
prerequisites.why: nuclear devices are mature, but shaping most of their energy into a narrow plasma jet has only been studied on paper.

prerequisites.tech: Shock absorbers for repeated huge impulses
prerequisites.why: gas-damped and hydraulic systems tested on the ground show the principle works, but nothing has run for thousands of pulses.
each pulse vaporises a thin layer of oil, so the plate is consumed slowly over the mission and needs a resupply of coating.

prerequisites.tech: Instrumentation and control for rapid pulse timing
prerequisites.why: firing something every second for months and keeping the thrust axis true demands reliable high-rate control electronics.

prerequisites.tech: Legal regime permitting nuclear detonations in space
prerequisites.why: treaties bar nuclear explosions in orbit and in space, so the concept cannot be flight-tested as the law stands.
a useful vehicle masses thousands of tonnes, far beyond any single launcher, so it must be assembled in orbit.

pathway.milestone: paper studies and small-scale conventional-explosive tests of plate and shock absorbers
pathway.unlocks: verified models of how a flat plate responds to a plasma impulse.

pathway.milestone: uncrewed pulse concepts that replace bombs with small magnetically compressed plasma rings
pathway.unlocks: a far lower-yield, repeatable pulse that is easier to test and to control.

pathway.milestone: a deep-space robotic demonstrator firing pulses outside protected orbits
pathway.unlocks: real flight data on thrust, ablation and structural fatigue.

pathway.milestone: crewed interstellar precursor moving at a few thousand kilometres per second
pathway.unlocks: reach to the outer solar system in months and to nearby stars over decades — if the legal and material barriers can be cleared.
